name: Royal jelly

lead: Royal jelly is the secretion nurse bees feed to queen larvae. It is sold as a supplement and used in cosmetics, promoted for vitality, smoother skin and a younger look.

It contains protein, sugars, lipids including 10-HDA and B vitamins, and proponents credit it with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. In bees, its proteins drive queen development. The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support human health benefits, and no trial has measured appearance.

paras: It is taken as capsules, fresh or freeze-dried jelly, or blended with honey, and it also appears in creams and serums. Users take it as a daily routine over weeks, often alongside other skin supplements.

Allergic reactions from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis have been reported, with higher risk in people with allergies. It is sold as a supplement, and the FDA has acted against unsupported health claims.

angle.text: Royal jelly is taken as a supplement and used in cosmetics for smoother, younger-looking skin, based on its bee-derived nutrients and proteins. EFSA reviewed the human health claims in 2011 and found no support.

lead: Royal jelly is a milky secretion produced by the head glands of young worker honey bees (Apis mellifera) and fed to all larvae in their first days and, throughout life, to queen larvae and adult queens.[1] It is harvested commercially and sold as a dietary supplement and cosmetic ingredient, and is used in apitherapy, the use of bee products in alternative medicine. In skin-care it appears in creams and serums marketed for hydration and anti-aging, and in oral products as a general wellness supplement.[2]

Its composition is roughly two-thirds water, with protein (largely major royal jelly proteins), sugars and lipids including 10-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid (10-HDA), plus B vitamins such as pantothenic acid.[1] Proponents credit it with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and rejuvenating properties, and reviews of bee products describe antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-aging activities from laboratory and animal work.[3][4][2] The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support health benefits in humans from consuming royal jelly.

A 2025 randomized, double-blind split-face trial of 70 Japanese women reported that a cream containing protease-treated royal jelly improved crow's-feet wrinkle depth, skin hydration and dermal thickness versus placebo over 12 weeks.[5][6] Allergic reactions ranging from hives to asthma and, rarely, fatal anaphylaxis have been reported with oral use.[7]
infobox: From queen cells about day 4; roughly 500 g per hive per season
EFSA (2011): evidence did not support human health claims

paras: Royal jelly is sold as fresh or freeze-dried product, capsules, powders, honey blends and as an ingredient in cosmetics.[2] Apitherapy practitioners and supplement makers promote it for vitality, skin quality, menopausal comfort and immune support, and a 2024 review lists vasodilatory, antioxidant, anti-aging, wound-healing and many other activities reported in experimental studies.[8]

Cosmetic formulations use royal jelly for moisturising and anti-aging claims; a 2020 review of bee products in dermatology says honey, propolis, royal jelly and beeswax are used in skin care and attributes antibiotic, anti-inflammatory, antiallergenic and anti-aging activities to royal jelly.[2] The compound 10-HDA is cited as a pharmacologically active constituent.[2]

Royal jelly appears in multi-ingredient supplement formulas discussed on lifting forums; one T Nation thread lists a leg-training formula with 50 mg of freeze-dried royal jelly standardised to 1.4% 10-hydroxydecenoic acid, and another thread quotes a book praising royal jelly as rich in B vitamins.[9][10] A 2022 randomized pilot trial in swimmers combined royal jelly with coenzyme Q10 and reported effects on exercise performance and markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage.[11]

Nurse bees secrete royal jelly from the hypopharyngeal and mandibular glands; larvae destined to be queens are fed it continuously, whereas worker larvae switch to a pollen and honey mixture after about three days.[1] Beekeepers harvest it from queen cells around the fourth day of larval life, and a well-managed hive may yield about 500 g over a five-to-six-month season.[1] A 2026 review notes high-yield bee lineages that produce up to ten times more royal jelly than Italian bees.[6]

Honey bee research has examined how this diet drives caste differences. A 2008 Science study reported that silencing the DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3 in larvae produced queen-like development, linking royal jelly to epigenetic control, a 2010 study mapped differential brain DNA methylation in queens and workers, and a 2011 Nature paper proposed that a royal jelly protein, royalactin, induces queen differentiation.[12][13][14] Wikipedia adds that newer research suggests the absence of certain nutrients fed to workers may matter as much as royal jelly itself. These are findings about bees, not humans.

Reference summaries give approximate proportions of 67% water, 12.5% protein, 11% sugars, 6% fatty acids and 3.5% 10-HDA; it lacks the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and contains pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6) and trace minerals. Major royal jelly proteins form a nine-member family; MRJP1, also called royalactin, is the most abundant, and MRJP1 to 5 make up 83 to 90% of the protein. The product is perishable and typically cold-stored or freeze-dried.[1] A 2025 C. elegans study found fresh royal jelly extended worm lifespan while samples stored at 4 C or 25 C did not, illustrating how freshness can alter activity in experiments.[6]

A 2025 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face study in 70 healthy Japanese women compared a protease-treated royal jelly cream with placebo for 12 weeks; the authors reported improved maximum and average crow's-feet wrinkle depth, higher stratum corneum water content and dermal thickness, and a decrease in cheek skin bacteria in the royal jelly group, with an ex vivo increase in the epidermal stem-cell marker COL17A1.[5][6] The authors describe it as the first study to show wrinkle-improving effects of this extract.[6]

Other randomized trials study oral royal jelly for non-appearance outcomes: a 200-woman Iranian trial of 1,000 mg daily for eight weeks reported lower menopausal symptom scores than placebo, and a randomized study examined bone metabolism in postmenopausal women.[15][16]

Reviews of honey-bee products summarise laboratory, animal and some human findings on antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, noting varied study quality.[3][17][4][18][8] Registered human trials examine hypertension, chronic kidney disease, coronary artery disease, male infertility and upper respiratory infections, many still recruiting or without posted results.[19][20][21]

Wikipedia reports that reactions range from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis, with unknown incidence and higher risk in people with other allergies. A 1993 Medical Journal of Australia case report described royal jelly-induced asthma, and 2025 and 2026 reviews of bee products and supplements describe IgE-mediated and delayed allergic reactions, with atopic people and beekeepers at greater risk.[7][6]

In 2011 the European Food Safety Authority concluded that evidence did not support health benefits in humans from consuming royal jelly. The US FDA has taken action against companies making unsupported health claims, including a 2010 seizure of misbranded products and a 2007 warning letter to Beehive Botanicals. The product is not vegan.

Royal jelly is mentioned on forums mainly as one item in stacks of bee products, such as pollen and propolis, taken for allergies or general wellness, and as an ingredient in supplement formulas.[9][10] Anecdotal reports of this kind have not been examined in published studies.

lore.intro: On lifting and looksmaxxing forums royal jelly is discussed as an add-on to supplement stacks and bee-product combinations rather than as a stand-alone product.[9][10]
